title: Color Me Confused
bodyHtml:
The information on this page is needed for both problem (C) and problem (D). Otherwise, problems (C) and (D) are not related — you don't need to solve either one in order to solve the other.

Languages and their speakers have many ways of describing colors — sometimes by comparing to well-known materials (copper hair, mustard wallpaper); sometimes using very specific terms (crimson ribbon); and sometimes using very broad terms (gray-blue sky). English has 11 “basic color terms”: white, gray, black, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, pink, and brown. However, other languages can have as few as two or as many as 12.

Below is a table showing eight objects and the basic color word that native speakers of 15 different languages might use to describe them.

In 1969, the anthropologist Brent Berlin and linguist Paul Kay proposed a set of rules about basic color terms. Five of them are given below in a simplified form, with the objects (ripe plum, ripe strawberry, etc.) replaced with the letters (A) to (H). Note that a word is described as unique if it is used to describe only one of the eight objects.

  1. Every language has at least two basic color terms, which distinguish between (A) and (B).
  2. If it has at least three, it uses different words for each of (A), (B) and (C). If it has only three, the same word is used for both (B) and (D).
  3. If it has at least five, it distinguishes between (B) and (D), and also has a unique word for (E).
  4. If it has at least six, it distinguishes (D) from (F).
  5. A language only has a unique word for (G) if it also has one for (H). If it does not have a unique word for (H), (G) will share a word with at least one of (A), (D) or (F).

Although these rules are no longer believed to be completely true for all languages, they do still describe most languages accurately. In particular, they describe all 15 languages in the table above.

C1. Determine which object each of the letters (A) - (H) refers to. Each of the eight objects corresponds to exactly one letter.

C3. For each of the blanks a. - c., choose all possible words from the list of options that the language might use to refer to that object, while still following rules 1-5. In each case, the options are all the words shown in the table in that language.

  • a. nye, wɔ, finge
  • b. sõa'ro, ewuro, ya'saro, ñiro, butiro
  • c. likañ, walin, minj-kimemb, muk, mosimb, tund

Information on the languages featured in problem (C) and problem (D) is below. Note that this information is not relevant for solving either problem.

Amuzgo, Tlapanec, and Zapotec are clusters of closely related Otomanguean languages spoken in Mexico by around 60,000, 150,000, and 500,000 people, respectively. Apinaye and Karajá are Macro-Jê languages spoken in Brazil by around 2000-3000 people each. Bassa and Bété are Kru languages. Bassa is spoken by around 600,000 people in Liberia, Ivory Coast and Sierra Leone. Bété is spoken by several thousand people in Ivory Coast, although the dialect used in this problem had only 50 remaining speakers in 1992. Ejagham and Nafaanra are Atlantic-Congo languages. Ejagham is part of the Bantoid subgroup, and is spoken by around 120,000 people in Nigeria and Cameroon. Nafaanra is part of the Senufo subgroup, and is spoken by around 90,000 people, mostly in Ghana. English is an Indo-European language with around 400 million native speakers, and close to 1.5 billion total speakers worldwide. Guambiano and Tsafiki are Barbacoan languages. Guambiano is spoken by around 20,000 people in Colombia. Tsafiki is spoken by around 2000 people in Ecuador. Hebrew and Lele are Afro-Asiatic languages. Hebrew is from the Semitic subgroup, and was extinct as a spoken language between the 5th and 19th century CE, although it continued to be used for religious purposes; now it has around 5 million native speakers, and around 9 million total speakers, primarily in Israel. Lele is from the East Chadic subgroup, and has around 26,000 speakers in Chad. Kalam is a Trans-New-Guinea language, spoken by around 15,000 people in Papua New Guinea. Kwerba is a Greater Kwerbic language spoken by around 2500 people in West Papua. Matsés is a Panoan language spoken by around 2000 people on the Peru-Brazil border. Ocaina is a Huitotoan language, spoken by around 50 people along the Peru-Colombia border. Seri is a linguistic isolate spoken by 700-1000 people in Mexico. Teribe is a Chibchan language spoken by around 3000 people in Panama and Costa Rica. Tucano is a Tucanoan language, spoken by around 12,000 people in Brazil and Colombia. Waorani is a linguistic isolate spoken by around 2000 people in Ecuador; more speakers may be living in uncontacted groups in Peru. Yakan is an Austronesian language, spoken by around 100,000 people in the Philippines. Yucuna is an Arawakan language, spoken by nearly 2000 people along the Miritiparaná river in Colombia.

questions.partPrompt: Determine which object each of the letters (A) - (H) refers to. Each of the eight objects corresponds to exactly one letter.
For each language, indicate whether its color words follow rules 1-5 (YES) or not (NO).
For each of the blanks a. - c., list ALL words from the given options that the language might use for that object while still following rules 1-5. Separate your answers with commas.
questions.promptHtml: a. Nafaanra, ripe banana — options: nye, wɔ, finge
b. Tucano, fresh grass — options: sõa'ro, ewuro, ya'saro, ñiro, butiro
c. Kalam, ripe strawberry — options: likañ, walin, minj-kimemb, muk, mosimb, tund

hints.text: Start by counting how many DIFFERENT words each row of the first table uses. Bassa uses only two, Bété and Ejagham use three, Hebrew uses eight different words for eight objects. The rules are organised by that count, so the small rows tell you about the earliest letters (A, B, C) and the big rows tell you about the last ones (G, H).

Each rule is a test you can run on any row. Rule 1 must hold for every language, rule 2 only for rows with three or more distinct words, rule 3 for five or more, rule 4 for six or more. Rule 5 is the tie-breaker for the last two letters: try one assignment, then check it against a language whose word for the ripe plum is used for nothing else. If that language still needs its sky word to be shared with something, your assignment is wrong.

Practice the counting method on a row that isn't asked about: Teribe uses six distinct words (dindin, sresren, shoylor, keson, sisi, pluplun), so rules 1-4 all apply to it. Since dindin covers ripe plum, clear sky AND deep ocean, and rule 4 forces D and F apart, at most one of those three objects can be D or F. Stacking constraints like this across several rows is what pins down the letters.

explanationHtml:
The big idea

Each row of the tables is one language's way of carving up the colour space. A language with two words lumps lots of objects together; a language with eight words separates almost everything. Berlin and Kay's claim is that languages don't add colour words in random order: there is a fixed sequence, so knowing how many words a language has tells you which distinctions it must already make. The letters (A)–(H) are that sequence.

Step 1: count the distinct words in each row

Bassa: 2 (hui, ziza). Bété and Ejagham: 3. Karajá and Matsés: 4. Apinaye, Tsafiki and Seri: 5. Guambiano, Teribe and Tlapanec: 6. English: 8. Hebrew: 8 (all different). Now each rule only applies to rows big enough to trigger it.

Step 2: rules 1 and 2 — snow, crow, strawberry

Rule 2 says a three-word language uses three different words for (A), (B), (C). Look at Bété: the three groups are {snow}, {strawberry, banana}, {plum, grass, sky, ocean, crow}. Ejagham groups them as {snow}, {plum, strawberry, banana}, {grass, sky, ocean, crow}. So A, B, C must take one object from each group — and the objects that stay in the same group in both languages are: snow alone; strawberry (with banana); and grass/sky/ocean/crow together.

Rule 3 says any language with five or more words has a unique word for (E) (a word used for that object and nothing else). Check every row with 5+ words: ripe banana always has its own word — Tsafiki laqueban, Apinaye ràràr, Seri kwassool, Guambiano uscuig, English yellow. Crow fails in Tsafiki (paban is also the ocean), snow fails in Tsafiki (fiban is also the sky), grass fails in Tlapanec (maxa is also the sky). So E = ripe banana. That means the "strawberry group" contributes strawberry to A/B/C.

Rule 2's second half: in a three-word language, (B) and (D) share a word. In Bété the crow's word kp is also grass, sky and ocean; snow (fee) and strawberry (zeli) are not. Whichever of grass/crow is in {A,B,C}, its partner has to be the other one. Suppose grass were A: rule 1 says every language separates A from B, and rule 2 would need B = crow to share a word with D — but in Bété grass and crow are the same word, contradicting rule 1 or rule 2. So grass is D and crow is in {A,B,C}. Then rule 2's B=D pairing in Bété (grass = kp) forces B = adult crow, leaving snow and strawberry for A and C.

Step 3: rule 5 — the sky, the plum, and the snow

Rule 5 has two parts. First: a unique word for (G) requires a unique word for (H). Second: if there is no unique word for (H), then (G) shares a word with (A), (D) or (F).

Only two objects are candidates for G/H: clear sky and ripe plum (banana, grass, crow, snow, strawberry are already spoken for or being decided). Test the assignment G = plum, H = sky using English: English blue covers both sky and ocean, so sky is not unique; then plum would have to share a word with A, D or F — but English purple is used for nothing else. That breaks the rule. So G = clear sky and H = ripe plum, which leaves F = deep ocean.

Now finish A and C with Tsafiki. Tsafiki's plum word luban also covers the strawberry, so H is not unique; rule 5 therefore requires the sky word fiban to be shared with A, D or F. fiban is sky + snow, and grass (D) and ocean (F) have other words — so snow must be A, and strawberry is C.

Final key: A = fresh snow, B = adult crow, C = ripe strawberry, D = fresh grass, E = ripe banana, F = deep ocean, G = clear sky, H = ripe plum. (This is Berlin and Kay's famous order: white, black, red, green, yellow, blue, then sky-blue, then purple.)

C2: testing six new languages

For each row, count distinct words, then run only the rules that apply.

  • Kwerba (4 words): snow (asiram) differs from crow (icem), satisfying rule 1; snow, crow, strawberry (nokonum) all different, satisfying rule 2 (and it has more than three words, so the B=D clause doesn't apply). Rules 3 and 4 need 5+ and 6+ words, so they're off. Rule 5: sky is not unique (asiram also = snow), and it shares with A (snow) — satisfied. YES.
  • Lele (4 words): snow bole differs from crow induwa differs from strawberry wile — satisfied. Rule 5: sky bore is not unique, and it shares with D (grass) — satisfied. YES.
  • Ocaina (6 words): rule 4 now applies and demands grass (D) differs from ocean (F) — but both are moxooso. Rule broken. NO.
  • Waorani (4 words): snow na'amae'ta differs from crow wintamo differs from strawberry opa'tawae — satisfied; rule 5: sky we'nedae not unique and shared with grass and ocean — satisfied. YES.
  • Yucuna (6 words): rule 4 again — grass and ocean are both ipureni. Rule broken. NO.
  • Zapotec (7 words): grass nu-ca' differs from ocean nu-asul, satisfying rule 4; banana nu-cach is unique and crow differs from grass, satisfying rule 3; sky is not unique but shares with grass (D), satisfying rule 5. YES.

C3: filling the blanks

a. Nafaanra, banana. The row already has three words (nye, wɔ, finge), and filling the blank with any of them keeps it at three. With exactly three words the rules ask: snow, crow and strawberry all different (finge, wɔ, nye — satisfied), and crow = grass (both wɔ — satisfied). Rules 3 and 4 don't apply, and rule 5 is satisfied because the sky word is shared with grass. Nothing the banana does can break any of this, so all three options work.

b. Tucano, grass. Five words, so rule 3 applies: banana must be unique, and crow differs from grass. Choosing ewuro would make the banana word non-unique — rule broken; choosing ñiro would make grass equal the crow — rule broken. The other three (sõa'ro, ya'saro, butiro) each keep the banana unique and grass distinct from crow, and rule 5 stays happy because the sky word ya'saro is shared with the ocean (F). Rule 4 is not triggered (only five words).

c. Kalam, strawberry. Six words, so rules 2, 3 and 4 all apply. Rule 2 needs snow, crow, strawberry to be three different words, ruling out tund (snow) and mosimb (crow). Rule 3 needs the banana word walin to stay unique, ruling out walin. The survivors likañ, minj-kimemb and muk all pass: grass (minj-kimemb) is still distinct from ocean (muk) for rule 4, and the sky word muk is never unique, so rule 5 is fine because it is shared with the ocean (F).
